title: Faith, hope and charity (CCC 1812–1829)
hook: three virtues given by God, and the greatest is charity

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Beatitudes: eight blessings that sound backwards and paint a portrait of Jesus. Your line was blessed are. Which one did you carry? Today, three words many people know from weddings. Day three hundred thirteen.

If you've been to a wedding, you've probably heard it. Someone's cousin walks up to the lectern, a little nervous, and reads: charity is patient, is kind. Or in other Bibles, love is patient, love is kind. Everyone nods. It sounds like it was written for the couple. It wasn't. Paul wrote it to a church in Corinth that was fighting: over leaders, over gifts, over who was more spiritual. And he ended with three words, and a ranking. The Church has built a whole teaching on those three, and calls them different from every other virtue.
screen: `A COUSIN AT THE LECTERN.` → `WRITTEN TO A CHURCH IN A FIGHT.` → `THREE WORDS, AND A RANKING.`

segments.voice: First, the verse, in the Douay-Rheims: "And now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three: but the greatest of these is charity." Second, why theological. Theos is Greek for God. The Catechism calls these the theological virtues because they come from God, are aimed at God, and are about God directly. Most virtues, like patience or courage, can be built by practice. These three, Catholics say, are given: poured in by God, first at baptism. We can grow in them, but we don't invent them. Third, the three. Faith is believing God and all he has revealed. Hope is desiring God's kingdom and eternal life, and trusting his promises, relying not on our own strength but on grace. The letter to the Hebrews calls hope "an anchor of the soul, sure and firm." Not optimism, which depends on how things look. Hope holds even when things look bad. And charity is loving God above all things, and our neighbor as ourselves, for God's sake. Fourth, why charity is greatest. In the Latin Bible it's caritas, in the Greek agape: not a feeling, not a donation, but a love that wills the good of the other. Paul describes it: "Charity is patient, is kind: charity envieth not, dealeth not perversely; is not puffed up." And he says why it's the greatest: faith and hope belong to this life. One day, Catholics say, faith will become sight and hope will be fulfilled. Charity is the only one of the three that never ends. It's what heaven is made of.
screen: `FAITH, HOPE, CHARITY: THESE THREE.` · `FROM GOD, AIMED AT GOD.` · `HOPE: AN ANCHOR, NOT OPTIMISM.` · `CHARITY NEVER ENDS.` · then, large: `THE GREATEST OF THESE IS CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: practice hope once today. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing that feels stuck: a worry, a relationship, a situation that isn't changing. Don't pretend it's fine. Hope isn't pretending. Just picture dropping an anchor beside it: something that holds, even while the water moves. If you pray, you can hand it to God, and let him hold the rope. If you don't, hold the image of the anchor for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Theological virtues. Faith, hope and charity: three virtues Catholics say are given by God and aimed at God, and the greatest of them is charity. Today's word.
Your line: the greatest is charity. Today, when you catch yourself worrying, drop the anchor once. And do one patient, kind thing for someone who won't notice. Day three hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Many Catholics pray short traditional acts of faith, hope and charity, and 1 Corinthians 13 is among the readings most often chosen for Catholic weddings.

fork.setup: Paul ranks faith, hope and charity. which does he call the greatest?
fork.reveal: the greatest of these is charity: faith becomes sight and hope is fulfilled, but charity never ends.

original.note: Greek: love that wills the other's good. Latin caritas, English charity.

trapdoor: what you thought: charity means giving money away.
what it means: loving God above all and neighbor as yourself, the greatest of three virtues given by God.
what a scholar hears: agape and caritas; the theological virtues as infused (CCC 1813); 1 Corinthians 13 written into a quarrel; charity as the virtue that remains.
